Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico’s girlfriend, Brianna Menard, was identified by her father, Matt Menard, during an undercover conversation in which he and Williamson County Democratic Chair Kim Collins Gilby separately cast doubt on Talarico’s recent moderate messaging on border security, immigration, and transgender surgeries for minors.

Menard, who claims to communicate with Talarico weekly and has personally discussed immigration policies with Talarico. Insisting James Talarico remains a progressive, opposes ICE’s immigration enforcement tactics, and supports a pathway to citizenship for everyone. Menard also warns against putting too much stock in Talarico’s public border security remarks.

Meanwhile, Collins Gilby suggests Talarico’s CNN town hall comments on transgender surgeries for minors were an attempt to appear more centrist to Texas voters, arguing that Democrats must first win elections to advance their priorities.

Inside Travis County Democratic Headquarters, regional organizer Andhi Beltran Garcia mentions that James Talarico is portraying himself as a moderate on issues like abortion to appeal to Texas voters while privately holding more progressive positions.

The undercover footage raises questions about whether Talarico’s moderate public messaging represents a genuine shift in his political positions or an effort to appeal to independent voters ahead of the U.S. Senate election.

We have reached out to James Talarico’s campaign, family & Texas Williamson County Democratic party for comment.

James O’Keefe on the Felony Charges for Exposing Fraud in Minnesota:  

This is not political. It is fundamental. It is about whether citizens still have the right to question their government. This is now a landmark First Amendment case, and every American’s right to speak truth to power has been put on the line.  

Weaponized lawfare does not work against me. It has always backfired on the people who come after me. Most people find criminal charges and lawsuits stressful; the process becomes a form of punishment. But I love this process because it gives me the opportunity to expose injustice at the highest levels. My foundation will be indemnifying members of the Justice League, including @camhigby for their lawful reporting. 

I’m calling on all Americans, and especially all journalists, to stand united on a message to the prosecutors in Minnesota: the politics of fear will not prevail in the United States of America.

O’Keefe confronted Abdoul Beckwith, a regional field organizer for Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, at the campaign's Detroit office following our undercover investigation into Beckwith's claims about overseas campaign contributions, Hamas, and the Muslim Brotherhood.

When O’Keefe questioned Beckwith about his previously recorded statements revealing El-Sayed receives donations from overseas, Beckwith became visibly agitated, repeatedly cursed at O’Keefe, and lunged toward him as another individual physically restrain him.

“I don't give a f* who you are, bro,”** Beckwith repeatedly shouted.

Campaign staff demanded O’Keefe and his team leave the premises, warning they would call the police.

“We're going to ask for one more time and then we're going to have to call the cops.”

Outside the campaign office, O’Keefe continued seeking answers about Beckwith's allegations as individuals inside appeared to block the windows.

Another individual confronted O’Keefe and accused him of racism. O’Keefe challenged the accusation while reiterating that his questions concerned potential violations of federal campaign finance law.

O'Keefe asks, “I want to know why the money is coming from overseas.”

Under 52 U.S.C. § 30121, foreign nationals are prohibited from contributing to federal campaigns. However, U.S. citizens living abroad and lawful permanent residents may legally contribute. Beckwith's allegations do not independently establish that illegal contributions occurred.

Following the confrontation, OMG received confirmation from the Michigan Democratic Party that Beckwith had been terminated from his position. O’Keefe has filed a police report in Michigan following the assault. The incident was documented under Police Report #2610150266.

We went undercover inside Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign, capturing conversations with Abdoul Beckwith, a regional field organizer for Abdul for Senate, discussing El-Sayed’s overseas campaign contributions, Hamas, and the Muslim Brotherhood.

Beckwith claimed El-Sayed receives donations from overseas, “You know, he [Abdul El Sayed] has people from overseas that donate to him.” When asked whether overseas donations were prohibited, Beckwith responded, “No it is not allowed,” before describing a hypothetical arrangement in which overseas money passes through a family member.

Beckwith said, “And then people overseas give money to him. And then he gives money to you. It's that type of thing.” He added, “Everybody does it!”

Under 52 U.S.C. § 30121, foreign nationals are prohibited from contributing to federal campaigns. However, U.S. citizens living abroad and lawful permanent residents may legally contribute.

During a car ride with our OMG undercover journalist, Beckwith suggested El-Sayed could lose support if he openly rejected Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood, “He [Abdul El Sayed] can't just say, you know, no, I don't support Hamas, you know, I reject all of them, because he's going to lose the people that brought him up in the first place.” Beckwith continued, “He [El-Sayed] has to play the game. He has to play the role.”

When questioned about the Muslim Brotherhood, Beckwith claimed denouncing the organization could alienate Muslim supporters, stating: “So that's the whole thing. So when Abdul is going to denounce that [Muslim Brotherhood], they're [Muslims] going to think that he is siding with the genociders.”

Beckwith also expressed concerns about the influence of white and Jewish individuals surrounding El-Sayed. Mentioned El-Sayed could adopt their “mannerisms.”

Beckwith: “There's a lot of white people around him [El-Sayed]. A lot of Jewish people around him. And when you're around a certain group of people for so long, you absorb the ideology, the mannerisms, everything like that.”

He warned, “They're [Whites & Jews] going to hijack him and then in a year he's going to be doing what they want with him.” When asked whether El-Sayed might abandon his promises, Beckwith responded, “I think, yeah.”

Beckwith also made an allegation about Secretary of State and gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson and stated "But I know Jocelyn works for the KKK." He repeated, "She works for the KKK. For the Ku Klux Klan."

In an unexpected moment, Beckwith recalled what he described as a previous encounter with Project Veritas during the 2020 Georgia Senate runoff campaign. “He had a backpack, but on his backpack, you could see a camera lens. You could see the red light of the camera lens.” Six years later, Beckwith was telling that story to another O’Keefe undercover journalist.

OMG has contacted Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign for comment and also contacted Bob Hobert, identified as an official with One Team Michigan whose role is to elect Abdul El-Sayed. We are now aware from the Michigan Democratic Party that Abdoul Beckwith has been terminated from his position.

These statements were captured on hidden camera by an OMG journalist inside the U.S. Senate campaign for Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit, Michigan.

After nearly five years, the Department of Justice has finally unredacted portions of the probable cause affidavit used to justify the FBI's November 5, 2021, raid on my home.

The newly revealed sections detail how federal investigators obtained my emails through Microsoft, examined internal newsroom communications, referenced my fingerprints from a 2010 arrest, and tracked my whereabouts before the raid.

Among the communications discussed was an email explaining why we chose NOT to publish Ashley Biden's diary over concerns about verification and journalistic ethics.

For years, I've demanded answers about why the federal government went to such extraordinary lengths to investigate journalists who never published the diary.

Now, we're finally getting a closer look at what they kept hidden.

Under Minnesota Statutes § 201.061, a registered voter can sign an affidavit affirming that they know another individual resides in the same precinct, allowing that person to register at the polls without presenting standard proof of residence. One registered voter can vouch for up to eight people.

O’Keefe and the team wanted to find out what this actually looks like inside a polling place and how far election workers would let them take it.

Disguised in traditional Muslim attire, O’Keefe and members of the team entered polling locations across Minneapolis and presented an intentionally extreme scenario to expose what they see as the sheer lunacy of Minnesota’s “vouching” system. O’Keefe told workers that the people accompanying him were unregistered and repeatedly pressed them about identification, how many people he could bring in, and what would be required for them to register.

Again and again, workers explained the vouching process to the team.

At one location, after O’Keefe made clear that the people with him were not registered, a worker told him he could vouch for as many as eight people. O’Keefe told the worker he would leave, get additional people, and return. The worker explained that because O’Keefe was already registered, he could serve as the voucher.

At another location, a poll worker explained that if everyone was in the same precinct and O’Keefe was already registered there, he could vouch for their residency.

When O’Keefe pressed her about identification, she put it plainly: “You’re the ID.”

At White Park Recreation Center, a worker explained that a voucher must personally know the individuals and know that they live within the precinct. The worker also explained that the voucher signs a legal oath affirming their residency, while the individuals being vouched for sign an oath affirming their own identity and eligibility to vote.

O’Keefe asked whether their eligibility was actually verified. “After the fact, yeah,” the worker responded.

The team wanted to put the process to an extreme real-world test and document what election workers would tell them when confronted with the scenario firsthand. The purpose wasn’t simply to ask what Minnesota law says on paper.

Not every worker reacted the same way.

Some became suspicious of the team and challenged what they were doing. But across the locations captured in the investigation, OMG documented workers explaining how Minnesota’s vouching process could be used to establish residency for people registering at the polls without standard identification.

The investigation is part of an ongoing @ctznjusticelg series, with additional follow-up reporting from @anthonyjrubin, founder of @realmuckraker, and @camhigby coming soon.

OMG obtained voter records showing multiple absentee-ballot return envelopes with individual Detroit voters. These records revealed discrepancies including different ballot numbers, different election-official initials, strikingly different signatures, and, in one case, separate voter identification numbers associated with the same name, birthdate, and address.

O’Keefe and OMG undercover journalists went door-to-door to locate the voters named on the envelopes and ask them directly about what the records showed. Michael Lynn Barnett was confronted with two return envelopes carrying different ballot numbers and different election-official initials. When O’Keefe asked about the records, Barnett responded, “What about it?” and later ordered him off the property. At another stop, Myrtle Harvey appeared to acknowledge the two absentee-ballot return envelopes, telling O’Keefe, “They must have sent me two,” and suggesting the city of Detroit had made a mistake.

The registered address associated with Margarett Alma Bass led OMG to an abandoned building. At Naomi Price’s home, O’Keefe attempted to ask why her name appeared on two return envelopes bearing different ballot numbers (4831 and 5490), but a family member refused to let the team speak with her. And at the final stop, Myranda Morrow did not recognize the second signature appearing on an absentee-ballot return envelope associated with her, raising the question of who signed it and why.

In the Myrtle Harvey case, OMG says its barcode scans produced two separate voter identification numbers despite the records carrying the same name, birthdate, and address. Her signatures on the two envelopes also appeared nearly identical. Being registered twice is not itself evidence that someone voted twice, and the existence of two return envelopes does not establish that two ballots were accepted. The records show discrepancies, but they do not tell us what ultimately happened to each ballot. To determine whether both ballots were counted or whether one was canceled, replaced, rejected, spoiled, or otherwise removed from the process, OMG is seeking the complete election records for each case.

To determine what actually happened with each ballot, OMG submitted written requests to the Detroit Department of Elections and the City of Detroit’s FOIA office for the complete voting and absentee ballot histories of the voters identified in the investigation.

OMG is also seeking ballot applications, replacement ballot requests, return envelopes, poll book records, counting board totals, ballot numbers, mailing and return dates, and records showing the final status of each ballot. These records should help determine whether each ballot was accepted, rejected, replaced, canceled, spoiled, or ultimately counted.

This case began after our January 2025 “Dating the Deep State” investigation series involving former FBI agent and federal contractor Jamie Mannina, who was recorded claiming he was having conversations with retired generals to “protect people from Trump.” Mannina, represented by @MarkSZaidEsq, later sued OMG and its undercover reporters for claims including defamation and false light, fraudulent misrepresentation, civil conspiracy, and federal wiretapping.

In July 2026, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta denied our motion to dismiss, allowing the case to proceed. Among the issues now being challenged is whether terms such as “Deep State” can be treated as provably false factual assertions rather than political characterization or rhetorical hyperbole. The order also discusses the word “coup,” but OMG’s position is that the word was never used in the published reporting; rather it appeared in Mannina’s own allegations about what our reporting supposedly implied.

Mannina also alleges fraudulent misrepresentation based on the undercover journalist’s use of a fabricated dating persona. Our argument raises a much bigger question for undercover journalism: Can concealing a journalist’s identity or motives to obtain information itself become legitimate actionable fraud?

That question is even more significant, especially since Judge Mehta’s order relied on Democracy Partners v. Project Veritas, a case that has recently produced a groundbreaking D.C. Circuit ruling. We have now asked the court to reconsider its decision in light of that new controlling appellate precedent.

Our newly filed motion argues that the recent Democracy Partners precedent changes the analysis: where protected publication contributes to the alleged injury, a plaintiff faces a heavy burden to establish that independently unlawful conduct, not the publication, was the force behind those damages the plaintiff sustained.

Here, there was no alleged workplace infiltration, theft of documents, entry into a private computer system, or access to a restricted government facility. According to his own filings, Mannina met someone at public restaurants and voluntarily spoke to her. Our position is that his alleged employment, reputational, and emotional injuries resulted from the subsequent publication of what he said, not simply from his reliance on a dating profile that may have been inaccurate.

And there is another federal ruling in another jurisdiction involving OMG with strikingly similar allegations: Fseisi v. O’Keefe Media Group. That case also involved Bumble, alleged false representations, purported romantic dates, secret recordings, a federal security contractor, and claims including fraudulent misrepresentation and wiretapping. Judge Anthony Trenga dismissed the fraud claim, concluding that the subsequent publication was an intervening cause of the claimed injuries.

This is bigger than one lawsuit. The question is whether traditional undercover newsgathering techniques can be repackaged as “fraud” when the alleged injury ultimately stems from publication protected by the First Amendment.

Under Minnesota’s Statutes § 201.061, a registered voter can sign an affidavit affirming that they know another individual resides in the same precinct, allowing that person to register at the polls without presenting standard proof of residence. One registered voter can vouch for up to eight people.

We wanted to find out what this actually looks like inside a polling place and how far election workers would let us take it.

Disguised in traditional Muslim attire, we entered polling locations across Minneapolis and presented an intentionally extreme scenario to expose the sheer lunacy of Minnesota’s ‘vouching’ system. I told workers that the people accompanying me were unregistered and repeatedly pressed them about identification, how many people I could bring in, and what would be required for them to register.

Again and again, workers explained the vouching process to us.

At one location, after I made clear that the people with me were not registered, a worker told me I could vouch for as many as eight people. I told them I would leave, get additional people and return. The worker explained that because I was already registered, I could serve as the voucher.

At another location, a poll worker explained that if everyone was in the same precinct and I was already registered there, I could vouch for their residency.
When I pressed her about identification, she put it plainly: “You’re the ID.”

At White Park Recreation Center, a worker explained that a voucher must personally know the individuals and know that they live within the precinct. The worker also explained that the voucher signs a legal oath affirming their residency, while the individuals being vouched for sign an oath affirming their own identity and eligibility to vote.

I asked whether their eligibility was actually verified. “After the fact, yeah,” the worker responded.

We wanted to put the process to an extreme real-world test and document what election workers would tell us when confronted with the scenario firsthand. The purpose wasn't simply to ask what Minnesota law says on paper.

Not every worker reacted the same way. Some became suspicious of our team and challenged what we were doing.
